danish.title: Anden bog (1805) — Kapitel 3
paragraphs: Da Kutuzov vendte tilbage fra revy'en, tog han den østrigske general med ind i sit private værelse og bad sin adjudant om nogle papirer vedrørende troppernes tilstand ved ankomsten samt brevene fra ærkehertug Ferdinand, der havde kommandoen over den fremskudte hær. Fyrst Andrej Bolkonskij kom ind med de ønskede papirer. Kutuzov og det østrigske medlem af Hofkriegsrådet sad ved bordet, hvor et kort var bredt ud.
»Ah!« sagde Kutuzov med et blik på Bolkonskij, som om han med det udbrud bad adjudanten om at vente, og fortsatte samtalen på fransk.

»Alt, hvad jeg kan sige, hr. general,« sagde han med en behagelig elegance i udtryk og tonefald, der fik lytteren til at hæfte sig ved hvert bevidst udtalt ord. Det var tydeligt, at Kutuzov selv lyttede med fornøjelse til sin egen stemme. »Alt, hvad jeg kan sige, hr. general, er, at hvis sagen afhang af mine personlige ønsker, ville Hans Majestæt kejser Franz' vilje for længst have været opfyldt. Jeg ville for længst have sluttet mig til ærkehertugen. Og tro mig på min ære, at det personligt ville være mig en glæde at overdrage den øverste kommando over hæren til en bedre informeret og mere dygtig general — af hvilke Østrig har så mange — og nedlægge hele dette tunge ansvar. Men omstændighederne er somme tider stærkere end os, hr. general.«

Og Kutuzov smilede på en måde, der syntes at sige: »De har fuld ret til ikke at tro mig, og det er mig endda ganske ligegyldigt, om De gør det eller ej, men De har ingen grund til at sige det til mig. Og det er hele pointen.«
Den østrigske general så utilfreds ud, men havde intet andet valg end at svare i samme tone.

»Tværtimod,« sagde han med en klagende og vred stemme, der stod i skarp kontrast til hans smigrende ord, »tværtimod, Deres Eksellences deltagelse i den fælles indsats er højt værdsat af Hans Majestæt; men vi mener, at den nuværende forsinkelse berøver de glimrende russiske tropper og deres fører de laurbær, de er vant til at vinde i deres slag,« sluttede han sin tydeligvis forberedte sætning.
Kutuzov bukkede med det samme smil.

»Men det er min overbevisning, og efter det seneste brev, som Hans Højhed ærkehertug Ferdinand har beæret mig med, forestiller jeg mig, at de østrigske tropper under så dygtig en leder som general Mack allerede har vundet en afgørende sejr og ikke længere behøver vores hjælp,« sagde Kutuzov.

Generalen rynkede panden. Skønt der ikke forelå nogen sikker efterretning om et østrigsk nederlag, var der mange omstændigheder, der bekræftede de uheldige rygter, og Kutuzovs antydning af en østrigsk sejr lød derfor meget som ironi. Men Kutuzov blev ved med blødt at smile med det samme udtryk, der syntes at sige, at han havde ret til at antage det. Og faktisk meddelte det seneste brev, han havde modtaget fra Macks hær, en sejr og erklærede, at hærens stilling strategisk set var meget gunstig.

»Giv mig det brev,« sagde Kutuzov og vendte sig mod fyrst Andrej. »Vær venlig at kigge på det« — og med et ironisk smil om mundvigene læste han følgende passage fra ærkehertug Ferdinands brev højt for den østrigske general på tysk:

Vi har fuldt koncentrerede styrker på næsten halvfjerds tusind mand til at angribe og besejre fjenden, skulle han krydse Lech. Da vi desuden er herrer over Ulm, kan vi ikke berøves fordelen ved at beherske begge sider af Donau, så skulle fjenden ikke krydse Lech, kan vi krydse Donau, kaste os over hans forbindelseslinjer, gå over floden længere nede og forpurre hans hensigt, skulle han forsøge at rette hele sin styrke mod vores trofaste allierede. Vi vil derfor med fuld tillid afvente det tidspunkt, da den kejserlige russiske hær er fuldt udrustet, og vil så i fællesskab let finde en måde at berede fjenden den skæbne, han fortjener.
Kutuzov sukkede dybt, da han var færdig med afsnittet, og kiggede mildt og opmærksomt på medlemmet af Hofkriegsrådet.

»Men De kender jo det vise mundheld, Deres Eksellence, der anbefaler, at man forbereder sig på det værste,« sagde den østrigske general, tilsyneladende ivrig efter at gøre en ende på spøgerierne og komme til sagen. Han så sig uvilkårligt om efter adjudanten.

»Undskyld mig, general,« afbrød Kutuzov, idet han ligeledes vendte sig mod fyrst Andrej. »Hør nu, min kære ven, hent alle rapporterne fra vores spejdere hos Kozlovskij. Her er to breve fra grev Nostitz, og her er et fra Hans Højhed ærkehertugen, og her er disse,« sagde han og overrakte ham flere papirer, »udarbejd et pænt notat på fransk ud fra alt dette, der viser alle de efterretninger, vi har modtaget om de østrigske troppers bevægelser, og giv det til hans eksellence.«

Fyrst Andrej nikkede som tegn på, at han fra første ord havde forstået ikke blot det, der var blevet sagt, men også hvad Kutuzov gerne ville have fortalt ham. Han samlede papirerne, bukkede for begge og gik lydløst hen over tæppet og ud i venteværelset.

Skønt der ikke var gået lang tid, siden fyrst Andrej forlod Rusland, var han forandret meget i den periode. I hans ansigtsudtryk, hans bevægelser, hans gang var der knap et spor tilbage af den tidligere affekterede slaphed og dovenskab. Han lignede nu en mand, der ikke har tid til at tænke over det indtryk, han gør på andre, men som er optaget af behageligt og interessant arbejde. Hans ansigt udstrålede mere tilfredshed med sig selv og omgivelserne, og hans smil og blik var lysere og mere tiltrækkende.

Kutuzov, som han havde indhentet i Polen, havde modtaget ham meget venligt, lovet ikke at glemme ham, udmærket ham frem for de andre adjudanter og taget ham med til Wien, hvor han betroede ham de mere alvorlige opgaver. Fra Wien skrev Kutuzov til sin gamle kammerat, fyrst Andrejs far.
Deres søn tegner til at blive en officer, der udmærker sig ved sin flid, fasthed og handlekraft. Jeg anser mig for heldig at have en sådan underordnet hos mig.

På Kutuzovs stab, blandt hans kolleger og i hæren i det hele taget, havde fyrst Andrej, ligesom i Petersborg-selskabet, to helt modsatte omdømmer. Nogle, et mindretal, anerkendte, at han adskilte sig fra dem selv og fra alle andre, ventede sig store ting af ham, lyttede til ham, beundrede og efterlignede ham, og i deres selskab var fyrst Andrej naturlig og behagelig. Andre, flertallet, brød sig ikke om ham og anså ham for indbildsk, kold og utiltalende. Men blandt disse folk forstod fyrst Andrej at hævde sig på en måde, så de respekterede og endda frygtede ham.
Fyrst Andrej kom ud af Kutuzovs værelse med papirerne i hånden og hen til sin kammerat, den vagthavende adjudant Kozlovskij, der sad ved vinduet med en bog.
»Nå, fyrste?« spurgte Kozlovskij.
»Jeg har fået ordre til at skrive et notat, der forklarer, hvorfor vi ikke rykker frem.«
»Og hvorfor er det?«
Fyrst Andrej trak på skuldrene.
»Nyt fra Mack?«
»Nej.«
»Hvis det var sandt, at han var blevet slået, ville der være kommet besked.«
»Sandsynligvis,« sagde fyrst Andrej og bevægede sig mod yderdøren.

Men i det øjeblik trådte en høj østrigsk general i en stor kappe, med Maria Theresia-ordenen om halsen og et sort bind om hovedet — tydeligvis netop ankommet — hurtigt ind og smækkede døren. Fyrst Andrej standsede brat.
»Øverstbefalende Kutuzov?« sagde den nyankomne general hurtigt med hård tysk accent, seende til begge sider og gående lige mod den indre dør.
»Den øverstbefalende er optaget,« sagde Kozlovskij og skyndte sig hen til den ukendte general for at spærre vejen til døren. »Hvem må jeg melde?«
Den ukendte general så nedladende ned på Kozlovskij, der var temmelig lav, som om det undrede ham, at nogen ikke kendte ham.
»Den øverstbefalende er optaget,« gentog Kozlovskij roligt.

Generalens ansigt formørkedes, hans læber bævede og rystede. Han tog en notesbog op, kradsede hastigt noget ned med blyant, rev bladet ud, gav det til Kozlovskij, gik hen til vinduet med hurtige skridt og kastede sig ned i en stol, mens han stirrede på de tilstedeværende, som ville han spørge: »Hvorfor ser de på mig?« Derefter løftede han hovedet, strakte halsen, som om han ville sige noget, men begyndte straks med påtaget ligegyldighed at nynne for sig selv og frembrage en underlig lyd, der øjeblikkelig brød af. Døren til det private værelse åbnedes, og Kutuzov viste sig i døråbningen. Generalen med det forbundne hoved bøjede sig frem, som om han flygtede fra en fare, og med lange, hurtige skridt på sine tynde ben gik han hen til Kutuzov.
»Vous voyez le malheureux Mack« (De ser den ulykkelige Mack), ytrede han med brudt stemme.

Kutuzovs ansigt, som han stod der i den åbne dør, forblev fuldkommen ubevægeligt i nogle øjeblikke. Så løb rynkerne over hans ansigt som en bølge, og panden blev atter glat; han bøjede ærbødigt hovedet, lukkede øjnene, lod tavst Mack gå ind i sit værelse foran sig og lukkede selv døren bag dem.

Rygtet, der var gået om, at østrigerne var blevet slået, og at hele hæren havde overgivet sig ved Ulm, viste sig at være sandt. Inden en halv time var adjudanter blevet sendt i alle retninger med ordrer, der viste, at de russiske tropper, der hidtil havde været uvirksomme, også snart ville komme i kamp med fjenden.

Fyrst Andrej var en af de sjældne stabsofficerer, hvis vigtigste interesse lå i krigens overordnede gang. Da han så Mack og hørte om hans katastrofe, forstod han, at halvdelen af felttoget var tabt, indså alle vanskelighederne ved den russiske hærs stilling og forestillede sig levende, hvad der ventede, og den rolle, han ville komme til at spille. Uvilkårligt følte han en glad ophidselse ved tanken om det hovmodige Østrigs ydmygelse, og at han måske om en uge ville se og deltage i det første russiske sammenstød med franskmændene, siden Suvorov mødte dem. Han frygtede, at Bonapartes geni kunne overgå de russiske troppers mod, og dog kunne han ikke udholde tanken om, at hans helt skulle lide vanære.

Ophidset og oprevet af disse tanker gik fyrst Andrej mod sit værelse for at skrive til sin far, som han skrev til hver dag. I korridoren mødte han Nesvitskij, som han delte værelse med, og spøgefuglen Zjerkov; de lo som sædvanlig.
»Hvorfor er du så trist?« spurgte Nesvitskij og bemærkede fyrst Andrejs blege ansigt og funklende øjne.
»Der er ikke noget at være glad for,« svarede Bolkonskij.

Netop som fyrst Andrej mødte Nesvitskij og Zjerkov, kom en østrigsk general, Strauch, der var tilknyttet Kutuzovs stab som ansvarlig for forsyningen af den russiske hær, gående imod dem fra den anden ende af korridoren, sammen med det medlem af Hofkriegsrådet, der var ankommet aftenen før. Der var plads nok i den brede korridor til, at generalerne let kunne passere de tre officerer, men Zjerkov skubbede Nesvitskij til side med armen og sagde åndeløst:
»De kommer! De kommer! Træd til side, gør plads, vær venlig at gøre plads!«

Generalerne passerede med et udtryk, som om de gerne ville undgå pinlige opmærksomheder. I spøgefuglen Zjerkovs ansigt viste der sig pludselig et dumt, tilfreds grin, han tilsyneladende ikke kunne undertrykke.
»Deres Eksellence,« sagde han på tysk, idet han trådte frem og henvendte sig til den østrigske general, »jeg har den ære at lykønske Dem.«
Han bukkede og skrabede først med den ene fod, så den anden, klodset som et barn til danseundervisning.

Medlemmet af Hofkriegsrådet så strengt på ham, men kunne ikke lade være med at give ham et øjebliks opmærksomhed, da han så det alvorlige i hans dumme smil. Han kneb øjnene sammen for at vise, at han lyttede.
»Jeg har den ære at lykønske Dem. General Mack er ankommet, ganske rask, bare lidt forslået lige her,« tilføjede han med et strålende smil og pegede på sit hoved.
Generalen rynkede panden, vendte sig bort og gik videre.
»Gott, wie naiv!« sagde han vredt, da han var kommet et par skridt væk.
»Herregu, hvor naivt!«

Nesvitskij slog med et grin armene om fyrst Andrej, men Bolkonskij, der blev endnu blegere, skubbede ham væk med et vredt blik og vendte sig mod Zjerkov. Den nervøse irritation, som Macks tilsynekomst, nyheden om hans nederlag og tankerne om, hvad der ventede den russiske hær, havde fremkaldt, fandt sit udløb i vrede over Zjerkovs malplacerede spøg.

»Hvis De, min herre, vælger at gøre sig til klovn,« sagde han skarpt med en let bæven i underkæben, »så kan jeg ikke forhindre Dem; men jeg advarer Dem om, at hvis De vover at spille nar i mit nærvær, skal jeg lære Dem at opføre Dem.«
Nesvitskij og Zjerkov var så overraskede over dette udbrud, at de tavst stirrede på Bolkonskij med vidåbne øjne.
»Hvad er der i vejen? Jeg lykønskede dem jo bare,« sagde Zjerkov.
»Jeg spøger ikke med Dem; vær så venlig at tie stille!« råbte Bolkonskij og tog Nesvitskijs arm og forlod Zjerkov, der ikke vidste, hvad han skulle sige.
»Hvad er der nu, gamle ven?« sagde Nesvitskij og forsøgte at berolige ham.

»Hvad der er?« udbrød fyrst Andrej og standsede i sin ophidselse. »Forstår du da ikke, at vi enten er officerer, der tjener vores zar og vort fædreland og glæder os over vores fælles sags sejre og sørger over dens ulykker — eller blot lakajler, der er ligeglade med deres herres anliggender? Quarante mille hommes massacrés et l'armée de nos alliés détruite, et vous trouvez là le mot pour rire,« sagde han, som om han styrkede sin holdning med denne franske sætning. »C'est bien pour un garçon de rien comme cet individu dont vous avez fait un ami, mais pas pour vous, pas pour vous. Kun et umodent pjok kan more sig på den måde,« tilføjede han på russisk — men udtalte ordene med fransk accent — da han bemærkede, at Zjerkov stadig kunne høre ham.
»Fyrre tusind mand massakreret, og vores allieredes hær tilintetgjort, og De finder det morsomt!«
»Det passer sig for den døgenigt, De har gjort til Deres ven, men ikke for Dem, ikke for Dem.«
Han ventede et øjeblik for at se, om kornetten ville svare, men han vendte sig og forlod korridoren.

english.title: Book Two (1805) — Chapter 3
paragraphs: Returning from the review, Kutuzov brought the Austrian general to his private room and, calling for his adjutant, asked for papers on the condition of the arriving troops and the letters that had come from Archduke Ferdinand, who commanded the advance army. Prince Andrew Bolkonsky entered the room with the requested documents. Kutuzov and the Austrian member of the Hofkriegsrath were sitting at a table with a map spread out before them.
[speaking in French] "Ah..." said Kutuzov, glancing at Bolkonsky as though asking the adjutant to wait, and went on speaking in French.

[speaking in French] "All I can say, General," he began with an elegant pleasantness of tone and delivery that made you want to listen to each carefully chosen word — it was clear Kutuzov enjoyed the sound of his own voice — "all I can say, General, is that if the matter depended solely on my personal wishes, His Majesty Emperor Francis's will would have been fulfilled long ago. I would have joined the Archduke without delay. And believe me, on my honor, it would be a genuine pleasure for me to hand over supreme command of the army to a more knowledgeable and capable general — of whom Austria has so many — and to lay down this heavy burden of responsibility. But circumstances are sometimes stronger than we are, General."

Kutuzov smiled in a way that seemed to say: You're perfectly free not to believe me, and I really don't care whether you do or not — but you have no grounds for calling me a liar. And that's the whole point.
The Austrian general looked displeased but had no choice except to respond in the same tone.

"On the contrary," he said in a querulous, irritated voice that clashed with his flattering words, "on the contrary — Your Excellency's participation in the joint effort is highly valued by His Majesty. But we believe this current delay is robbing the splendid Russian troops and their commander of the laurels they have so often won in battle." He finished what was clearly a rehearsed speech.
Kutuzov bowed, wearing the same smile.

"But that is my conviction, and judging by the most recent letter with which His Highness Archduke Ferdinand has honored me, I would assume the Austrian forces, under the direction of so skilled a commander as General Mack, have already won a decisive victory and no longer require our assistance," said Kutuzov.

The general frowned. Although there was no confirmed news of an Austrian defeat, too many troubling rumors were circulating for comfort, and Kutuzov's cheerful mention of an Austrian victory sounded suspiciously like sarcasm. But Kutuzov went on smiling blandly with the same expression — as if he had every right to think so. And in fact, the most recent dispatch from Mack's army had reported a victory and described the army's strategic position as highly favorable.

"Let me see that letter," said Kutuzov, turning to Prince Andrew. "Have a look at this" — and with an ironic smile playing at the corners of his mouth, Kutuzov read aloud to the Austrian general the following passage, in German, from Archduke Ferdinand's letter:

We have fully concentrated forces of nearly seventy thousand men with which to attack and defeat the enemy should he cross the Lech. Also, as we command Ulm, we cannot be deprived of the advantage of holding both sides of the Danube, so that should the enemy not cross the Lech, we can cross the Danube, throw ourselves on his line of communications, recross the river further downstream, and frustrate his intentions should he try to direct his whole force against our faithful ally. We shall therefore confidently await the moment when the Imperial Russian army is fully equipped, and shall then, in conjunction with it, easily find a way to deliver the enemy the fate he deserves.
Kutuzov sighed deeply when he finished reading and looked at the Hofkriegsrath member with a mild, attentive gaze.

[speaking in French] "But you know the wise maxim, Your Excellency — always prepare for the worst," said the Austrian general, clearly wanting to move past the sarcasm and get down to business. He glanced involuntarily at the aide-de-camp.

[speaking in French] "Excuse me, General," Kutuzov interrupted, also turning to Prince Andrew. "Here's what I need, my dear fellow: get all the scout reports from Kozlovsky. Here are two letters from Count Nostitz, and here's one from His Highness Archduke Ferdinand, plus these" — he handed over several papers — "put together a clean memo in French summarizing everything we know about the Austrian army's movements, then deliver it to His Excellency."

Prince Andrew nodded to show he had understood from the first word — not only what was said, but what Kutuzov actually meant behind it. He gathered the papers and, with a bow to both men, stepped quietly across the carpet and into the anteroom.

Although not much time had passed since Prince Andrew left Russia, the change in him was remarkable. In the expression on his face, in his gestures, in the way he walked, almost no trace remained of his former mannered laziness and indifference. He now looked like a man who has no time to think about the impression he makes on others because he is absorbed in meaningful, engaging work. His face showed more contentment with himself and those around him; his smile and his eyes were brighter, more appealing.

Kutuzov, whom he had caught up with in Poland, had received him warmly, promised not to forget him, singled him out from the other adjutants, and brought him along to Vienna, entrusting him with the more important assignments. From Vienna, Kutuzov had written to his old comrade, Prince Andrew's father:
Your son gives every promise of becoming an officer distinguished by his diligence, resolve, and competence. I consider myself fortunate to have such a subordinate at my side.

On Kutuzov's staff, among his fellow officers and in the army at large, Prince Andrew had — just as in Petersburg society — two sharply opposite reputations. A minority recognized him as someone different from themselves and everyone else, expected great things of him, listened to him, admired and imitated him. With these people, Prince Andrew was natural and at ease. The majority, however, disliked him and thought him arrogant, cold, and unpleasant. But among this group, Prince Andrew knew how to carry himself in a way that commanded their respect and even their fear.
Coming out of Kutuzov's room with the papers in hand, Prince Andrew walked up to his comrade Kozlovsky, the aide-de-camp on duty, who was sitting by the window reading a book.
"Well, Prince?" Kozlovsky asked.
"I've been ordered to write a memo explaining why we aren't advancing."
"And why aren't we?"
Prince Andrew shrugged.
"Any news from Mack?"
"No."
"If he'd really been defeated, we'd have heard by now."
"Probably," said Prince Andrew, and started toward the outer door.

But at that instant, a tall Austrian general in a greatcoat strode in quickly, slamming the door behind him. He wore the Order of Maria Theresa around his neck and had a black bandage wrapped around his head. He had obviously just arrived.
"Commander in Chief Kutuzov?" the newcomer demanded, speaking quickly in a harsh German accent, looking both ways and heading straight for the inner door.
"The commander in chief is in a meeting," said Kozlovsky, hurrying up to block his path. "Whom shall I announce?"
The unknown general looked down at the rather short Kozlovsky with contempt, as if astonished that anyone could fail to recognize him.
"The commander in chief is in a meeting," Kozlovsky repeated calmly.

The general's face darkened. His lips trembled. He pulled out a notebook, scribbled something in pencil, tore out the page, thrust it at Kozlovsky, then strode to the window and threw himself into a chair, glaring around the room as if to ask: Why are they all staring at me? He raised his head and stretched his neck as though about to speak, but then, with forced indifference, began humming to himself — and the odd sound broke off almost immediately. The door to the private room opened and Kutuzov appeared in the doorway. The general with the bandaged head jerked forward as if fleeing some danger and, taking long, rapid strides on his thin legs, rushed up to Kutuzov.
[speaking in French] "You see before you the unfortunate Mack," he said in a broken voice.

Kutuzov's face, framed in the open doorway, remained completely still for several seconds. Then a wave of wrinkles passed across it, his forehead smoothed again, and he bowed his head respectfully, closed his eyes, silently let Mack walk past him into the room, and shut the door behind them both.

The rumor that the Austrians had been crushed and that the entire army had surrendered at Ulm turned out to be true. Within half an hour, adjutants were being dispatched in every direction with orders that made it clear the Russian army, inactive until now, would soon have to face the enemy.

Prince Andrew was one of those rare staff officers whose deepest interest lay in the overall course of the war. When he saw Mack and heard the details of the catastrophe, he immediately grasped that half the campaign was already lost. He vividly understood the full difficulty of the Russian army's position and could picture exactly what lay ahead and what role he would have to play. In spite of himself, he felt a surge of excitement at the thought of arrogant Austria's humiliation, and at the prospect that within a week he might witness — and take part in — the first clash between Russian and French forces since the days of Suvorov. He feared that Napoleon's genius might overwhelm Russian courage, yet at the same time he could not bear the thought of his hero being disgraced.

Agitated and unsettled by these thoughts, Prince Andrew headed to his room to write to his father, as he did every day. In the corridor he ran into Nesvitsky, with whom he shared quarters, and the joker Zherkov. As usual, they were laughing.
"Why so grim?" Nesvitsky asked, noticing Prince Andrew's pale face and glittering eyes.
"There's nothing to be cheerful about," Bolkonsky answered.

Just as Prince Andrew encountered Nesvitsky and Zherkov, two men approached from the other end of the corridor: Strauch, an Austrian general on Kutuzov's staff who oversaw provisioning for the Russian army, and the Hofkriegsrath member who had arrived the previous evening. The corridor was wide enough for the generals to pass the three officers without any difficulty, but Zherkov shoved Nesvitsky aside and said in a breathless voice:
"They're coming! They're coming! Step aside — make way, please, make way!"
The generals walked past, clearly trying to avoid any awkward attention. On Zherkov's face there suddenly appeared a stupid grin of delight that he seemed unable to suppress.
[speaking in German] "Your Excellency," he said, stepping forward and addressing the Austrian general, "I have the honor of congratulating you."
He bowed and began scraping first one foot and then the other, clumsy as a child at a dance lesson.
The Hofkriegsrath member eyed him severely, but the earnest stupidity of that beaming smile made it impossible to ignore entirely. He narrowed his eyes to show he was listening.
"I have the honor of congratulating you. General Mack has arrived — perfectly well, just a little bruised right here," Zherkov said, pointing to his own head with a radiant smile.
The general scowled, turned away, and walked on.
[speaking in German] "God, how childish!" he muttered angrily after a few steps.
"Good God, what simplicity!"

Nesvitsky threw his arms around Prince Andrew with a laugh, but Bolkonsky — turning even paler — shoved him away with a furious look and rounded on Zherkov. The anxious irritation triggered by Mack's appearance, the news of his defeat, and the thought of what awaited the Russian army all found an outlet in rage at Zherkov's ill-timed joke.

"If you choose to make a buffoon of yourself, sir," he said sharply, his lower jaw trembling slightly, "I can't stop you. But I warn you: if you dare to play the fool in my presence, I will teach you how to behave."
Nesvitsky and Zherkov were so stunned by this outburst that they stared at Bolkonsky in silent, wide-eyed shock.
"What's the matter? I was only congratulating them," Zherkov said.
"I am not joking with you — be quiet!" Bolkonsky snapped, and taking Nesvitsky by the arm, he walked away from Zherkov, who stood there not knowing what to say.
"Come on, what's gotten into you?" Nesvitsky said, trying to calm him.

"What's gotten into me?" Prince Andrew burst out, stopping in his tracks, his voice shaking with emotion. "Don't you understand? Either we are officers serving our Tsar and our country, who share in its victories and grieve at its misfortunes — or we are nothing but servants who couldn't care less about their master's business. [speaking in French] Forty thousand men slaughtered and the army of our allies destroyed, and you find that amusing! [speaking in French] That's fine for some worthless nobody like that creature you've made your friend, but not for you — not for you. Only a juvenile could find entertainment in this," he added in Russian, though he used the French-accented word for juvenile, noticing that Zherkov could still hear him.
"Forty thousand men massacred and the army of our allies destroyed, and you find that a cause for jesting!"
"It is all very well for that good-for-nothing fellow of whom you have made a friend, but not for you, not for you."
He waited a moment to see if the cornet would respond, but Zherkov turned and walked out of the corridor.
